t: Celtic religion was polytheistic: the names of over two hundred deities survive, among them Lugus, Toutatis, Taranis, Cernunnos, Epona and Belenos, and several gods were seen as threefold.
Its priests were the druids, and its rites were held in sacred groves called nemetons, at springs and in timber temples, with offerings, often of weapons, thrown into rivers, lakes and bogs.
Almost everything known of it comes from archaeology, from Greek and Roman writers who were often hostile, and from medieval Irish and Welsh tales written down by Christian monks.
dyk: In Ireland the satire of a gifted poet was a serious curse: the filid, visionary poets and keepers of lore, were also magicians, for Irish magic was bound up with poetry.
ev: The Warrior of Hirschlanden is made in what is now Germany, one of the rare Celtic monumental stone sculptures from before the Roman conquest
The Celts begin to strike coins, copying Greek and Roman models, with heads and horses that may have had religious meaning
Rome conquers Gaul, and Celtic religion there blends with Roman religion into a syncretic Gallo-Roman faith
Rome conquers southern Britain, where Iron Age sacred sites are reused for Roman temples
The Coligny calendar, the oldest attested Celtic calendar, is made in Roman Gaul
The Gauls begin gradually to convert to Christianity
The Celtic peoples of Britain and Ireland begin gradually to convert to Christianity
The church in Ireland has relegated the druids to irrelevancy, while the filid keep much of their pre-Christian learning and status

f.origin: Among the Celtic peoples of Iron Age Europe, as a descendant of Proto-Celtic paganism, itself derived from Proto-Indo-European religion; its earliest monumental sculptures, from Germany, date to the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.
f.founder: none: it grew from older Indo-European religion, and many of its gods have cognates in other Indo-European mythologies.
f.scriptures: none written: the Celts wrote nothing down about their religion; it is known from archaeology, Greek and Roman writers, and Irish and Welsh tales written down by Christian monks in the Middle Ages.
f.followers: none: it died out as the Celtic peoples converted to Christianity, in Gaul from the 3rd century and in Britain and Ireland from the 5th; Celtic neopaganism, a 20th-century new religious movement, draws on it.
